indicators.note: inversely means turned the other way about, so the word for the blemishes is read from its end back to its start

blocks.note: warts are small hard growths on the skin

explanation.surface: A farmer's field of cornstalks set against a person's spotty complexion.
explanation.walkthrough: WARTS read backwards gives STRAW.
explanation.definitionFit: Straw is the dried stalks left after cereal crops such as wheat are harvested.

clue.text: Have a shot at this; you want the right pitch to start with.

blocks.note: the setter's reading: the thing aimed at in archery or shooting

blocks.clueFragment: you want the right pitch to start with
blocks.note: the surface reading sounds like tuning or a cricket wicket; the setter means the word itself opens with tar, which is pitch

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' suggests a cricket wicket or a musical note; it is the black sticky substance, whose other name begins the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An archer or rifleman aims at the marked board, so it is what you have a shot at.

clue.text: These people are much in the limelight.

definitions.text: These people are much in the limelight

blocks.note: the surface reading: celebrities constantly in the public eye
the setter's reading: limelight was the stage lighting of old theatres, so the people literally stand in it

explanation.walkthrough: Limelight was a bright stage lamp before electric light, so performers on stage are literally in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage performers stood under the bright quicklime lamps that lit Victorian theatres.

blocks.note: a plain definition: narrow at the middle like a wasp

explanation.definitionFit: The insect with a pinched middle gives an adjective for a figure with a very narrow middle.

clue.text: This arranges loans of varying interest.

definitions.text: This arranges loans of varying interest

blocks.note: the surface reading: a bank or moneylender
the setter's reading: interest means how engaging the books are, not a rate charged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Loans' and 'interest' point to banking; the loans are borrowed books, and their interest is how readable they are.
explanation.definitionFit: A public lending institution lends out books, some gripping and some dull, free of charge.

blocks.note: a plain definition: John Citizen is the ordinary man in the street, and his pet hate is what the government takes from him

explanation.definitionFit: Payments levied by government on ordinary people are the classic grievance of the average householder.

blocks.note: the surface reading: sticks for lighting fires, or things that pair up
the setter's reading: international cricket fixtures, the five-day kind

explanation.walkthrough: Test matches are full international cricket games, played over several days.
explanation.definitionFit: International cricket fixtures between national sides are given this name, as are examinations.

blocks.note: a plain definition: a command to pay heed

explanation.definitionFit: As a command, the verb means pay heed or listen carefully, like the exclamation demanding notice.

blocks.note: a plain definition: young eels, which will grow into adults

explanation.definitionFit: The young of the fish swim upriver as tiny transparent juveniles before growing to full size.

blocks.note: the surface reading: like a tired person
the setter's reading: a deep gap is said to yawn, meaning gape open

explanation.walkthrough: 'Yawns' suggests tiredness, but to yawn also means to gape wide, as a deep gorge does.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep gaping cleft in the earth is described as yawning open, yet has no need of rest.

clue.text: A political one mustn't be wooden.

definitions.text: A political one mustn't be wooden

blocks.note: the setter's reading: the body of senior ministers that runs a government
the surface reading: a piece of furniture with shelves or drawers is usually made of wood, but this kind must not be stiff and lifeless

explanation.walkthrough: The word means both a cupboard, normally wooden, and a group of ministers, who should not be wooden in the sense of dull and stiff.
explanation.definitionFit: The senior ministers who head a government form a body named after the private room where advisers once met.

blocks.note: a plain definition: absolute rulers, especially of Russia

explanation.definitionFit: The emperors of Russia held absolute power, so their title is a byword for despots.

clue.text: Suppose Yorkshire had eleven of these!

definitions.text: Suppose Yorkshire had eleven of these!

blocks.note: the surface reading: imagine a whole Yorkshire cricket team made up of one kind of player
the setter's reading: copies of George Hirst, the great Yorkshire all-rounder of the day

explanation.walkthrough: George Hirst was a famous Yorkshire cricketer, an all-rounder; a cricket team has eleven players, so eleven of him would make an unbeatable side.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the plural of a celebrated county cricketer's surname, imagined filling every place in the team.

clue.text: You will find these poles in music.

definitions.text: You will find these poles in music

blocks.note: the setter's reading: wooden poles or rods, one sense of the word
the surface reading: the five-line sets on which notes are written are known by the same word

explanation.walkthrough: The word means both stout sticks and the plural of the musical stave, the lines that carry the notes.
explanation.definitionFit: Staffs of wood and the ruled lines of written music share one plural noun.

blocks.note: a plain definition: to function or run

explanation.definitionFit: A machine that works is one that runs or functions, a verb synonym in the mechanical sense.

blocks.note: a plain definition: a fortified Spanish wine often served dry

explanation.definitionFit: Fino and amontillado are well-known dry styles of this fortified wine from Jerez in Spain.

clue.text: There are about two and a half acres in this, but you will only be able to find one.

definitions.text: There are about two and a half acres in this

blocks.clueFragment: There are about two and a half acres in this
blocks.note: the setter's reading: the metric unit of land area, equal to roughly 2.47 acres

blocks.clueFragment: you will only be able to find one
blocks.note: the surface reading seems a contradiction; the joke is that the word itself contains acre once, not two and a half times

explanation.walkthrough: The metric land unit holds about two and a half acres, but its spelling hides only one 'acre'.
explanation.definitionFit: The metric measure of land is ten thousand square metres, roughly two and a half imperial acres.

definitions.note: No definition is printed: early Times anagram clues gave only the letters to rearrange, and this marker stands where a definition would be

indicators.note: the old abbreviation printed after the words tells the solver outright that their letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of both words, taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: Early Times puzzles printed some clues as bare anagrams with no definition; the answer, meaning frets or complains, is simply the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: There is no definition; the answer means grumbles discontentedly or frets.

clue.text: A sleeping partner, perhaps, though far from being a silent one.

definitions.text: A sleeping partner, perhaps, though far from being a silent one

blocks.note: the surface reading: in business a sleeping partner puts in money but takes no active part, and is also called a silent partner

blocks.clueFragment: far from being a silent one
blocks.note: the setter's reading: a bedfellow who makes a great deal of noise in sleep

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sleeping partner' looks like the business term; read literally it is the person sharing your bed, and a noisy one at that.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who breathes loudly and roughly while asleep is the opposite of a quiet companion in bed.

blocks.note: a plain definition: a waterproof coat

explanation.definitionFit: A coat of cloth treated to repel rain, worn by sailors and fishermen.

clue.text: Arrangement of troops in step formation.

definitions.text: Arrangement of troops in step formation

blocks.clueFragment: Arrangement of troops in step formation
blocks.note: a plain definition: units placed in staggered parallel lines

explanation.definitionFit: Military units are placed in parallel rows, each set back from the one before like stairs.

blocks.note: a plain definition: deals out or allots by measure

explanation.definitionFit: The old verb meaning to allot or apportion survives mainly in the phrase about dealing out punishment.

blocks.note: a plain definition: a scrap of leftover food

explanation.definitionFit: This old word for a scrap or leftover morsel of food is a crossword favourite.

blocks.note: the surface reading: the only cheerful thing about a dreary place
the setter's reading: a fertile green place with water amid the sand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bright spot' is the idiom for a single cheering feature; here it is a literal green place in the sand.
explanation.definitionFit: A watered fertile patch in an arid sandy region is the traveller's only relief.

blocks.note: a plain definition: a principle or doctrine held as true

explanation.definitionFit: A principle or belief held by a group, such as an article of faith set out formally.

blocks.note: the surface reading: as if describing something squashed or dull
the setter's reading: thin circular plates, which are both flat and round

explanation.definitionFit: Thin circular plates, such as gramophone records or quoits, are by nature level and circular.

blocks.note: a plain definition: the person to whom money is paid

explanation.definitionFit: On a cheque the person named to receive the money is so called, the counterpart of the payer.

clue.text: Holds an established position in the church.

definitions.text: Holds an established position in the church

blocks.note: the surface reading: as if about a clergyman with a secure living
the setter's reading: a fixed bench seat that literally holds worshippers in place

explanation.walkthrough: 'Established' hints at the Established Church of England, but the thing is a fixed bench that holds the congregation.
explanation.definitionFit: A long fixed bench for worshippers stands in the nave of a place of worship.

blocks.note: the setter's reading: an immeasurably long age
the surface reading: a vast span packed into a single unit; the setter's joke is that the word uses exactly the letters of 'one'

explanation.walkthrough: The three letters of the answer are those of 'one' rearranged, which is the joke of 'in one'.
explanation.definitionFit: An immensely long period of time, an age beyond counting, is described by this short word.

blocks.note: the setter's reading: lashes of the whip given as punishment
the setter's reading: chevrons sewn on a uniform sleeve to mark rank or good conduct

explanation.walkthrough: The same plural noun means strokes of a lash, once a punishment, and the bands on a soldier's sleeve won by promotion.
explanation.definitionFit: Lashes from a whip and chevrons of rank on a sleeve are both called by this word.

blocks.note: a plain definition: making more sound

explanation.definitionFit: A comparative adjective for making more din, so a direct synonym in the same comparative form.

blocks.note: a plain definition: to make or become wider

explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to increase something in breadth, a straightforward synonym pairing.

blocks.note: first meaning: abandons, a verb
second meaning: barren regions without vegetation, a noun

explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a plural of leaf, set against 'leafless'; it is the verb, to abandon.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for abandoning someone and a noun for arid barren wastes.

blocks.note: a plain definition: the airy spirit who serves Prospero in Shakespeare's play

explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's play features an airy spirit freed by the magician Prospero, serving him on the island.

blocks.note: the setter's reading: the common venomous snake of Britain, also called the viper
the surface reading: the setter's reading is that the snake's letters rearrange to a word for great fear, the very feeling it inspires

explanation.walkthrough: Rearranged, the snake's name spells DREAD, which is what it inspires.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain's only venomous snake, the viper, is commonly known by this name.

clue.text: Split this aim and you will be under cover.

blocks.note: the setter's reading: a word for purpose, which divides into two words

blocks.clueFragment: and you will be under cover
blocks.note: the surface reading: the two halves read as being inside a canvas shelter

explanation.walkthrough: Split after its second letter the answer reads IN TENT, inside a canvas shelter.
explanation.definitionFit: A purpose or goal one means to achieve is a noun synonym for a target or object.

clue.text: The end is half the story in this case.

blocks.note: the setter's reading: the second half of the word is END, the first LEG
the surface reading: as if the ending were half of a tale; the answer is a traditional tale

explanation.walkthrough: The answer splits evenly into LEG and END, so 'end' really is half of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional tale handed down from the past, perhaps historical but unverifiable, is a kind of narrative.

blocks.note: the setter's reading: a social group or clique
the surface reading: as if someone were being praised as clever; the fashionable people form the smart one

explanation.walkthrough: 'The smart set' is the phrase for fashionable society.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of people with shared tastes is so called, and the fashionable crowd is known by that phrase.

clue.text: This gets cut up and should be replaced.

definitions.text: This gets cut up and should be replaced

blocks.note: the surface reading: sounds like something damaged or a person upset
the setter's reading: a piece of turf hacked out by a golf club, which etiquette says must be put back

explanation.walkthrough: Golfers are expected to replace the chunk of turf their club tears out of the fairway.
explanation.definitionFit: A clod of grass gouged from the ground by a golf stroke is the thing players are asked to put back.

clue.text: You hear it everywhere in denmark.

definitions.text: You hear it everywhere in denmark

blocks.note: the surface reading: as if a sound or rumour were common
the setter's reading: the national language spoken there

explanation.definitionFit: The Scandinavian language spoken throughout that kingdom takes its name from the country's people.

blocks.note: a plain definition: the face or its expression

explanation.definitionFit: Both nouns are literary words for a person's face and its look or expression.

blocks.note: a plain definition: brief and concise, sometimes curtly so

explanation.definitionFit: Speech that is brief and concise, using few words, often brusquely so.

blocks.note: first meaning: duller, slower-witted
second meaning, with 'heavier in' carried over: more compact and weighty

explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavier in' serves both halves: a slower intellect, or a more solid physical substance.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative means more stupid of a person and more closely packed of matter.

blocks.note: a plain definition: reproves angrily, an old sense of the verb

explanation.definitionFit: An old verb meaning to berate or chide angrily, unrelated to the noun for a charge or price.

blocks.note: a plain definition: relating to dogs

explanation.definitionFit: The adjective from the Latin for hound describes anything belonging to or like the family of hounds.

blocks.note: a plain definition: surrenders or hands over, especially territory

explanation.definitionFit: A formal verb for surrendering rights or territory to another party, as in a treaty.

definitions.note: No definition is printed: early Times anagram clues gave only the letters to rearrange, and this marker stands where a definition would be

indicators.note: the old abbreviation printed after the words tells the solver outright that their letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of both words, taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: Early Times puzzles printed some clues as bare anagrams with no definition: the answer, men who keep gates, is simply the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: There is no definition; the answer means the keepers of entrances at a ground or level crossing.

clue.text: You should be able to see through this.

definitions.text: You should be able to see through this

blocks.clueFragment: You should be able to see through this
blocks.note: the surface reading: as if about a window or a transparent excuse
the setter's reading: a small reinforced hole in fabric or leather, which can literally be looked through

explanation.walkthrough: 'See through' suggests a pane or a flimsy lie, but the thing is a little hole for a lace, and its name contains 'eye'.
explanation.definitionFit: A small round hole, edged with metal, for a lace or cord to pass through.

blocks.note: a plain definition: low backless sofas of Middle Eastern origin

explanation.definitionFit: These backless sofas take their name from the Turkish council chamber lined with cushioned benches.

clue.text: A bed of these is no place to sleep in.

definitions.text: A bed of these is no place to sleep in

blocks.note: the surface reading: a bed suggests sleeping, but here it is a patch of plants

blocks.clueFragment: is no place to sleep in
blocks.note: the setter's reading: stinging weeds would make a painful mattress

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bed' means a garden patch, not furniture; a patch of stinging weeds is the last place to lie down.
explanation.definitionFit: These stinging weeds grow in dense patches, and lying among them would be agony.

blocks.note: the surface reading: like an animal that slips its leash
the setter's reading: the small fasteners that once held detachable shirt collars, notorious for rolling away when dropped

explanation.walkthrough: Detachable shirt collars were fixed with small buttons that famously vanished under furniture once out of the collar.
explanation.definitionFit: Collar fasteners of the period were tiny buttons that rolled away as soon as they were removed.

clue.text: He makes footwear of a distress signal.

definitions.text: He makes footwear of a distress signal

blocks.note: the setter's reading: a blacksmith who fits horses' feet
the surface reading: SOS, whose letters with two more added make SHOES

explanation.walkthrough: The man who fits horseshoes 'makes footwear'; the joke is that the letters of SOS, padded out, spell what he makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A farrier who nails iron plates to horses' hooves is named for the thing he fits.
